newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION-S.AFRICA'S STATE PENSION FUND - BY E.OSBORN.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-S.AFRICA'S STATE PENSION FUND - BY E.OSBORN.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd

According to the Income Statement for the official pension and provident funds, as published in the Reserve Bank's Quarterly Bulletin, current benefits and administrative expenses of the funds are in balance with contributions.
This means that the entire interest and dividend income of the funds is available for investment.

The funds are managed by the Public Investment Commissioner (PIC). The total book value of funds administered by the PIC amounted to 127 billion rand at the end of 1996, of which 118.5 billion rand was attributable to the pension and provident funds of the public sector.

The analysis of assets shows that the PIC held 74.4 billion rand of government stock altogether, but this would be at book value. The total nominal value of PIC holdings of local registered stock actually amounted to 86.9 billion rand at this date.
The interest earned by the PIC in a full year on this government stock amounts to 10.6 billion rand, with negligible accrued interest on a very small holding of zero-interest stock.

Of this, 7.85 billion rand will be paid out in August and February, primarily because of the servicing in those months on the substantial holdings of the 13.5 percent R157, 13.0 percent R153 and 12.0 percent R150 -- 68 percent, 26 percent and 40.4 percent of totals issued, respectively.
Thus, there will be nearly four billion rand government interest paid to the PIC in August alone.

Such interest flows could be regarded as a captive source of funding the government's deficit in the past but, with the new policies of more active management of the funds in order to improve their actuarial balance, this is no longer the case. The pension and provident funds are wanting to increase their exposure to equities and minimise the reinvestment in government stock.
Given the magnitude of the flows as already indicated the implications are of some significance.

Not the entire 10.6 billion rand could be diverted to equities for, presumably, income for funds other than the pension funds administered by the PIC will still have to be plowed back into bonds. But on a proportionate basis 93 percent of the flows, identifiable with the pension funds, would be eligible for the equity market -- that is, a flow of 9.9 billion rand, say 10 billion rand.

The diversion of these funds will, naturally, have consequences both to the bond market and to the equity market. But the impact on markets can be reduced or even negated by the volumes of foreign portfolio investments in South African and of resident investments abroad following the relaxation of exchange controls.

Firstly, government funding operations for 1997/98 were estimated in the budget as involving 25 billion rand new monies, that is excluding redemptions which are normally rolled over. The actual requirements will, no doubt, be greater as revenue expectations were optimistic in view of the reduced GDP growth rate and expenditures are clearly to be exceeded, if only at the provincial level.
But much of this could be compensated for by privatisation proceeds flowing into the state coffers being substantially greater than budgeted.

After allowing for the budgeted net two billion rand short term loans, four billion rand foreign loans and nearly two billion rand from the transfer from the strategic fuel fund and the sales of state assets, some 17 billion rand new monies will have to be raised in the domestic market this financial year.

This would, undoubtedly, be a cakewalk if the 10 billion rand interest flows were available to government but not as evident in its absence. The estimates of state debt costs in this year's budget were based on the not unreasonable assumption of an average capital market yield of 15 percent and an average coupon rate on new government stock issues of 13.0 percent.
On this basis the total interest bill was estimated at 38.5 billion rand and the discount costs on stock issued at 5.3 billion rand.

A shortage of the supply of loanable funds in the market would manifest itself in a higher yield on stock issues and, in effect the same thing, a higher discount cost -- and hence a resultant higher level of public debt at the end of the financial year.

Such pressures have not emerged as yet. Furthermore, it is a fair presumption that they won't because of the volume of foreign funds flowing into the markets, sufficient to match the 10 billion rand and the outflow of institutional funds.

The latter results from the authorisation to invest abroad up to three percent of their net inflow of funds during 1996, possibly of the order of 60 billion rand, and a questionable further two percent for the purchase of stock listed in Southern African Development Community stock exchanges. The institutional outflow is thus not likely to exceed two billion rand.

So far this year foreign net purchases of gilts have amounted to 12.5 billion rand, but this includes an unknown substantial amount of swaps with South African institutions. The scale, however, suggests that the foreign contribution to the squaring of the funding circle will be sufficient.

On the other hand. the potential further 10 billion rand added to the flow of funds into the equity market will represent a positive boost to that market coming on top of the foreign portfolio flow. This has been 9.5 billion rand, to date, but is also inclusive of asset swaps. In 1994 some 37 billion rand went into the equity market in total, thus these additional funds will have a significant impact and buoy up the market in a current situation of sagging interest.

In sum, the strength of foreign participation in the South African financial markets has not only permitted considerable relaxation of exchange controls, but it has also made possible, fortuitously, the diversion of investible funds of the state pension funds from the gilt market to the equity market.
Furthermore, there will be a self-fulfilling validation of the new investment policies of the funds in that equity prices will be strengthened.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
